title: Poison at the river
hook: the cousins grow up under one roof, and envy grows with them until it reaches for poison
carry: matsarya: envy, one of the six enemies
tomorrow: a girl, a sage's mantra, and the rising sun.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti's mantra called Dharma, Vayu and Indra. A mantra: sacred words that call the divine.

A fruit tree in a royal garden, boys up in its branches reaching for fruit. Below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He kicks the trunk, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit. In the water he holds his cousins under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget.
screen: `A TREE FULL OF COUSINS.` → `BHIMA KICKS THE TRUNK.` → `DURYODHANA DOESN'T FORGET.`

segments.voice: The story moves fast now. Madri has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest. In the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five brothers to Hastinapura, and two families of cousins share one palace. Bhima beats them all, and Duryodhana, the story says, burns with jealousy. So he holds a day of water games by the Ganga, poisons Bhima's food, ties him as he sleeps, and pushes him into the river. Bhima sinks to the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. Their bites work against the poison, the Naga king welcomes him, and he comes home stronger. Vidura tells Kunti to say nothing in public, for her other sons' sake. Hindu teachers have a name for what grew in Duryodhana. The tradition counts six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, moha, which we met with his blind father, pride, and matsarya, envy. Matsarya is the pain of watching someone else have what you want. Notice it doesn't start as poison. It starts with a boy on the ground under a fruit tree, watching his cousin win. Fed every day, it grows into a plan. The tradition calls it an enemy because it lives inside you and fights you. Today it's a cousin's acceptance letter, a friend's post, a sibling praised at dinner. The feeling comes. The question is whether you feed it.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE PALACE.` · `POISON AT THE RIVER.` · `RESCUED AMONG THE NAGAS.` · `SIX INNER ENEMIES.` · then, large: `MATSARYA: ENVY.`

segments.voice: The Yoga Sutra, an old Hindu guide to the mind, offers a cure: meet the happy with friendliness. Bring to mind someone who has something you wanted. Notice the sting, and name it: matsarya. Then wish them well, once, plainly: may it go well for you. If you pray, ask God's blessing on them. If you don't, just let the wish stand.
Naga, the serpent people below the waters, whose venom worked against the poison envy put in Bhima's food.
Your line: matsarya, envy, one of the six enemies. It started under a fruit tree. Tomorrow, a secret older than all the cousins.

notes: All paraphrase. Days 722–726 were not on disk when this was written; this day takes the cousins' boyhood (Bhima's play, the poisoning, the Naga realm) as the close of the arc. If an earlier day already told the poisoning, this day needs a new angle.
Confirm in Ganguli: Bhima's rough play (shaking boys from trees, ducking them in water, dragging them) and the text's statement that it was without malice.

Confirm: Duryodhana binds the sleeping Bhima and throws him into the Ganga; the snakes' venom counters the poison; the Naga king (Vasuki, with Aryaka) gives him a strength-giving drink. Numbers in the source (bowls drunk, days slept, strength of elephants) are deliberately left out.
Confirm Vidura's counsel to Kunti to keep silent, and Yudhishthira's advice to his brothers to say nothing and guard one another.
